extracted.intended_audience: EPA writers and communicators (press officers, public affairs staff, product authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, consistent, plain-language EPA public communications (press releases, fact sheets, reports, web content) following AP-based EPA style. Covers grammar, punctuation, structure, tone, process and agency-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core style: Use the Associated Press (AP) Stylebook
rubrics_metrics.description: At its core, EPA style is simply the AP Stylebook; EPA follows AP for the great majority of grammar and usage questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA maintains an online AP subscription; AP updates conventions. Use AP as primary reference for punctuation, capitalization, numbers, etc., except where EPA modifies or supplements AP in this guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Always spell out 'United States' when it appears as a noun; 'U.S.' is acceptable as an adjective. State abbreviations are appropriate only in long lists, addresses, or with city names; use non-Postal abbreviations (e.g., 'Ala.,' 'Ariz.') with city names; eight states are never abbreviated in text; use two-letter Postal codes only in full addresses with ZIP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rules: 'Southwest' is one word; compass points abbreviated like 'SW'. Follow AP conventions and this EPA supplement for when to abbreviate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acronyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms are acceptable if spelled out the first time they appear. 'EPA' is a proper noun and should be used without 'the' in front (use 'EPA will...' not 'The EPA will...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out on first use; thereafter use the acronym alone. Treat 'EPA' as a proper noun in sentence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ampersands (&)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ampersands only when they are part of a formal name or when space is at a premium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'C & O Railroad' acceptable; otherwise use 'and'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bylines and staff credits
rubrics_metrics.description: GPO regulations confine bylines in government publications to authors of articles and photographers. 'Author' applies to the person who conceived or is responsible for the text; supervisors, advisors, or committee members should be listed under acknowledgments, not as authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledgements permitted (not thanks/dedications). Contractor staff names discouraged; contractor firm naming discouraged unless necessary; contract numbers may be listed. EPA is responsible for contractor work once published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize generic terms like 'waste management', 'disposal', 'pollution prevention', 'project', or chemical names. Capitalize only first word and proper nouns in titles and lists. Capitalize 'Agency' only when referring specifically to EPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules: lowercase 'federal, state, tribal' unless part of an official title; capitalize 'Internet' as a proper noun; capitalize 'Region' when referring to EPA Region offices (e.g., 'EPA Region 10') but not when referring to geographic regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use required disclaimers when materials include non-EPA authors' opinions, drafts, or references to commercial products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For non-EPA authors: include statement that views are authors' own and don't necessarily reflect EPA. Draft documents: 'This text is a draft...' Commercial references: state that mentioning trade names does not convey EPA endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider diversity in developing every communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure communications reflect diverse perspectives and are inclusive in content and representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-neutral language (Gender bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use gender-neutral words and avoid gender-biased language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult sources like the U.S. Department of Labor's Dictionary of Occupational Titles or Rosalie Maggio's The Nonsexist Word Finder for alternatives and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers and numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Per AP: spell out whole numbers below 10; use figures for 10 and above, with common exceptions (e.g., ages, percentages, monetary amounts). Spell numbers at the beginning of sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a 5-year-old girl', '3 percent', '6 cents'; sentence-starting numbers should be spelled: 'Twelve program offices...'. Follow AP exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice: Prefer active over passive
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active voice as much as possible; active sentences are stronger, clearer, and more actionable than passive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Passive 'A cleanup plan will be issued this summer.' Active: 'EPA will issue a proposed cleanup plan this summer.' Active voice helps identify actors and aids clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must use plain language in communications with the general public and specialized groups so audiences can understand on first read or hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plain language is defined by results—easy to read, understand, and use. Use GSA plain language resources and apply 'key elements of structure' (lead with main idea, clear organization, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most readers don't know what 'Region 1' means; list states or use regional descriptions and use Arabic numerals (e.g., 'Region 5'). Use 'EPA regional offices' instead of 'EPA regions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Region 5 (IL, IN, MI, MN, OH, WI)' and prefer 'EPA New England' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling: one word vs. two
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow AP/EPA preferences on word joins: e.g., 'cleanup' (noun/adjective), 'clean up' (verb); 'email' (not e-mail); 'groundwater' (one word); 'listserv'; 'online'; 'stormwater'; 'water body' (two words); 'website', 'webcam', 'webcast', 'webmaster'—AP conventions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hyphenated or alternate forms contrary to AP/EPA preference; use Webster's first spelling as EPA's official spelling guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles (levels and formatting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrict titles to two levels (main title and one subtitle). Use a colon for subtitle in references; ensure a key word appears near the beginning for clarity and bibliographic needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On covers indicate subtitle by spacing and lighter type. Use generic phrases in subtitles (e.g., 'Report to Congress') rather than in the main title for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common word-usage errors and confusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid frequent mistakes (affect/effect, bad/badly, compose/comprise, dispose/dispose of, good/well, figuratively/literally/virtually, impact vs affect, misuse of 'may', migrate usage, that/this, that/which, waste pluralization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples and correct forms (e.g., 'Acid rain affects trees' vs 'acid rain's effects...'; 'compose' vs 'comprise' distinctions; 'may' denotes permission not possibility). Use clear wording to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for kids (educational materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing materials for children/students/educators, consult EEWW and NAAEE guidelines emphasizing fairness and accuracy, depth appropriate to development, skills-building, action orientation, instructional soundness, and usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials should be fair and accurate, present diverse perspectives, foster understanding and critical thinking, promote civic responsibility, use sound instructional techniques, be well-designed and adaptable, and include instructor support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation pointers
rubrics_metrics.description: Special punctuation guidance supplements AP: apostrophe uses (PCBs plural not possessive), serial comma rules (AP recommends against serial comma except in specific exceptions), hyphen usage (compound adjectival hyphens before nouns), one space after periods, quotation marks and punctuation placement, semicolon usage, and punctuation for bulleted/vertical lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AP generally omits serial comma but use it for clarity or complex series; periods followed by one space; semicolons to join independent clauses or complex series items; follow Chicago for certain vertical lists with internal punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar guides: agreement, conjunctions, prepositions, split infinitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain pronoun-antecedent and subject-verb agreement; traditional avoidance of sentence-beginning conjunctions and sentence-ending prepositions is acknowledged but EPA allows exceptions when effective; split infinitives are not banned but seldom recommended; elliptical sentences may be effective but are grammatically incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, prefer formal constructions, make subjects clear, and rewrite to avoid awkwardness. Use parallel construction in complex sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and style recommendations (clarity first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity is the most important quality. Key structural elements: consistency, coherence, direction/integration, and plain language. Use parallel construction, concise sentences, subheadings, and strategic planning to make intent and message clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write tight—short sentences where possible; vary sentence length; if long sentences are necessary, surround with short ones. Consistent voice and spelling across a product are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to structure communications: hierarchy of interest (lead first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure communications using the hierarchy of interest: begin with the lead/key selling point/main theme—the idea of greatest audience interest—then expand. Summarize at the end when appropriate and tailor structure to audience and medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic lead should include who/what/when/where/how. Chronological, dramatic, and logical structures have limited uses; hierarchy-of-interest is generally most effective for busy audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: affirmation, person, voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone must be appropriate to content. Use positive statements, active voice, and second person where possible to be friendly and interactive; press releases and technical documents often use third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use positive constructions to avoid cognitive backtracking ('Leave the valve open' vs 'Do not close the valve'). Choose second or third person based on content sensitivity and audience. Tone shapes how readers judge the communicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid borrowed style (mimicking popular campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simply copy popular advertising or celebrity styles; what works for one organization may not work for EPA and copying is uncreative and potentially ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If entertainment serves a clear action or communication goal, use it deliberately; otherwise avoid mimicry and prioritize originality aligned to goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés, jargon, and 'hip' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clichés, jargon, and trendy 'hip' talk except when used intentionally and effectively for humor; jargon alienates broad audiences and undermines plain language goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain, accessible wording; if jargon is necessary, explain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition vs redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (intentional restating) can be a useful communication tool in teaching and marketing; redundancy is unnecessary repetition and should be avoided in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition purposefully to reinforce key points; avoid needless redundancy that adds no value.

rubrics_metrics.name: No self-aggrandizement
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must not promote the Agency, officials, or budgets for self-interest; federal law prohibits using appropriated funds for self-aggrandizing communications. Reports should not be promotional pieces that omit failures or mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge contributors for contact or credibility but avoid congratulations/dedications. Success stories should be presented honestly with proper attribution and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience; inclusiveness and appropriate depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what your audience wants and needs; be inclusive and avoid condescension. Provide appropriate depth for the audience—newcomers may still want detailed information presented simply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target specific audiences but ensure materials can be understood and used by the broad universe of stakeholders; tailor tone, structure, and depth accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive and probabilistic statements (be specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague subjunctive phrasing that implies speculative risk without context (e.g., 'This chemical can cause cancer' is meaningless without circumstances or probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting possibilities, explain the conditions or probabilities that make the statement true. Don't use subjunctive to create impressions of knowledge where none exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process suggestions: planning and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Brainstorm, outline, consider audience and medium, involve product review officers and program reviewers from concept stage, and consult available resources during development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For fact sheets aim for one page; decide whether humor/storytelling appropriate; involve product review officers early and view product review officer listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with main message in first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your main message (purpose statement and intended audience) in paragraph one; press-release leads should include who/what/when/where/how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should know immediately what they are expected to learn and why it benefits them; journalists' lead conventions apply for press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing, proofreading, and readability checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Always spell-check and proofread for typographical errors; have at least one other editor review the work; use readability tools (Flesch-Kincaid) and check readability statistics in Word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell-check misses many errors (their/there/they're, affect/effect, etc.). Use AutoCorrect to guard against frequent mistakes. In final review remove unnecessary words and verify names, acronyms, and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: Use AP Stylebook and Webster's Dictionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the AP Stylebook as the primary reference for style and Webster's (Merriam-Webster Collegiate) as EPA's official spelling guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA maintains AP subscription; Webster's first spelling is preferred (Merriam-Webster, 11th Ed.). Use these as authoritative references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance of style: Accuracy, honesty, and openness
rubrics_metrics.description: Honesty is the primary constituent of EPA communications. Communications must be truthful, whole, and clear so audiences can 'get it right.' Verification and coordination within the Agency are essential to avoid contradictions or the appearance of contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite sources, detail research, explain bases for statements. Use Communications Product Review and coordination processes to ensure internal consistency and to verify accuracy before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias for action (action orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications should reflect the public nature of EPA's work and often have a bias for action to involve and enable public participation and behavior change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell audiences how the communication benefits them and how to act; provide usable information that leads to decisions or actions (not merely information for information's sake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusiveness as a core value
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must convey information everyone can understand and use; target specific audiences but ensure materials are accessible to the broader public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exclusive language or assumptions; aim for democratic access to information and usability across populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and verification processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two critical steps for accuracy are coordination (ensuring consistency across Agency communications) and verification (confirming factual accuracy and also verifying to the audience by citing sources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established coordination mechanisms (Communications Product Review) and verify facts during writing; provide citations and explanations so audiences can evaluate claims.
